problemText: Which group of words is a fragment? Remember: a complete sentence needs a subject, a verb, and a finished thought.
choices: The cat jumped onto the shelf.
Maria wrote her name in the notebook.
Because the game got rained out.
The bell rang loudly at the end of class.
hints: Look for a starter word like because, although, when, or since that leaves the thought unfinished.
Test each group: does it have a subject AND a verb AND a finished thought?

problemText: Read this sentence. The storm knocked down the power lines we had no electricity for three hours. What is the problem, and which fix is best? Choose the option that correctly identifies the error and provides the best correction.
choices: It is a comma splice. Fix it: The storm knocked down the power lines, so we had no electricity for three hours.
It is a fragment because it lacks the necessary punctuation to separate two complete thoughts that belong in different sentences.
It is a run-on sentence that should be joined with the word and to show the connection between the two independent clauses.
It is a run-on sentence formed by pushing two complete sentences together without any punctuation or joining word between them.
hints: First, check: are there two complete sentences pushed together? Test each part for subject, verb, and finished thought.
The joining word you choose should match the meaning—what is the relationship between the power lines falling and losing electricity?

problemText: Which sentence is written correctly?
choices: The recipe called for flour the store was out of it because supplies had been limited all week.
After we planted the seeds in the spring, they grew into tall sunflowers by summer.
Whenever my alarm goes off I always feel groggy and tired throughout the entire morning.
The coach explained the new rules the team listened carefully and took notes on everything said.
hints: Look for a starter word at the beginning. If one is there, is there a comma after it, and does a complete sentence follow?
Test sentences that have no starter words: do they have two complete sentences smooshed together with no punctuation or only a comma between them?

problemText: Read this piece of writing. Although the playground equipment needed repairs. The students still had fun at recess. What is wrong with this writing, and how should it be fixed? You must choose the option that correctly names the error and gives a fix that works.
choices: There is a run-on sentence formed by two complete thoughts joined without any punctuation between them or a comma splice that needs a joining word.
There is a comma splice that requires a stronger joining word: Although the playground equipment needed repairs; therefore, students still had fun at recess.

There is a fragment because a starter word (although) is left standing alone. Attach it to the complete sentence with a comma: Although the playground equipment needed repairs, the students still had fun at recess.
There are two fragments in a row that need a coordinating conjunction between them to create a single compound sentence with proper structure.
hints: A starter word like although makes a promise—the thought is not finished until it connects to a complete sentence.
When the starter-word group comes first, what punctuation attaches it to the sentence that follows?

problemText: Which revision fixes both the sentence error and preserves the exact meaning that was intended?
choices: The school library closed at three o'clock we had to return our books early. (Use a semicolon.)
The school library closed at three o'clock we had to return our books early. (Use the word and.)
The school library closed at three o'clock we had to return our books early. (Use the word so.)
The school library closed at three o'clock we had to return our books early. (Use a period.)
hints: The sentence has two complete ideas with no punctuation between them. What kind of error is that?
Think about what each joining word means: and adds ideas equally; so shows cause-and-effect; but shows contrast. Which meaning does your sentence need?

problemText: A student wrote: Since the fire alarm went off during lunch. Nobody finished eating. Then she tried to fix it by moving the starter word to the end, like this: Nobody finished eating since the fire alarm went off during lunch. Is her fix correct? Explain why or why not, using the rules for starter words that you learned.
choices: Yes, her fix is correct. A starter word can come first or last, and when it comes last, no comma is needed.
No, her fix is still wrong because a starter word always needs a comma no matter where it is placed.
No, her fix is still wrong because the sentence now has too many ideas and cannot be fixed by moving the word.
Yes, her fix is correct, but she could also have fixed it by adding the word because between the two ideas.
hints: Reread the rule for starter words in both positions: what does the lesson say about comma placement when the starter word comes LAST instead of FIRST?
The lesson shows an example: 'We were late because the printer jammed.' Is there a comma? Does the starter word still work?

problemText: What does it mean when a paragraph has sentence variety? Which sentence best shows what sentence variety is?
choices: Mixing different sentence lengths and sentence openers so the writing does not sound like the same pattern repeating.
Using only long sentences with fancy vocabulary words and complex structures to impress the reader with greater sophistication.
Changing the meaning of the facts and details so they become more interesting and entertaining to read.
Making every sentence start with a different character's name instead of repeating the same character's name throughout the paragraph.
hints: Think about what the lesson said sentence variety changes — the shape, or the meaning?
Does variety mean swapping in new words, or does it mean mixing up how sentences are built and where they start?

problemText: Read this short passage: "The ball rolled down the hill. It hit the fence. It bounced back onto the grass." What is the first word of each sentence in order?
choices: Hill, fence, grass.
The, It, It.
Ball, it, it.
Rolled, hit, bounced.
hints: Look at the very first word of each sentence — the word that starts each one.
The first sentence starts with 'The', the second with 'It', and the third with 'It'. Can you spot the repeated word?

problemText: Which revision of these two sentences adds a connector that states the relationship between them? "The rain started. Everyone opened their umbrellas."
choices: The rain started, and it was raining hard when everyone opened their umbrellas.
When the rain started, everyone opened their umbrellas.
The rain started very suddenly. Everyone opened their umbrellas right away.
Everyone opened their umbrellas because the rain had started.
hints: A connector is a word like 'when', 'because', or 'as soon as' that shows how two ideas connect.
Look for a choice where one of those connector words joins the rain starting to the umbrellas opening, without adding new facts.

problemText: This paragraph has both a repeated opener and an unstated relationship: "The bell rang. The students lined up at the door. The teacher checked the attendance sheet." Which revision fixes both problems?
choices: The bell rang and rang. The students lined up at the door very quickly. The teacher checked the attendance sheet with great care.
The bell rang. When the students lined up at the door, the teacher checked the attendance sheet.
After the bell rang, the students lined up at the door, and then the teacher checked the attendance sheet.
When the bell rang, students lined up at the door, and the teacher checked the attendance sheet.
hints: First, spot the repeated opener — which word starts all three sentences? A real fix must remove that repetition or change where at least one sentence starts.
Second, look for a choice that adds a connector word (like 'when') to show the relationship between the bell ringing and what came after it.

problemText: A student wrote: "The timer went off. The cookies were burning. We pulled them out fast." The teacher says this needs variety but the facts are fine. Which statement best explains what fix would work here?
choices: Combine the first two sentences using a connector word that shows timing, and change where at least one sentence starts so 'The' and 'We' are not all the openers.
Add more adjectives to describe the cookies and timer and the baking sheet so the sentences sound longer and less repetitive in their rhythm.
Keep all three sentences separate but reorder them so the shortest sentence comes last and creates a better emphasis on the action.
Change 'The timer went off' to 'Our timer went off' and 'The cookies were burning' to 'Our cookies were burning' so patterns shift.
hints: Look at the openers: 'The', 'The', 'We' — are any of these the same word repeated three or more times in a row?
Even though two are the same, one job a real fix does is add a connector that states how the timer, the burning, and pulling them out are linked.

problemText: A writer has two versions of a paragraph about a game. Version 1: "The score was tied. The ref blew the whistle. Everyone froze. Everyone held their breath. The final shot went in." Version 2: "The score was tied when the ref blew the whistle, and everyone froze and held their breath. The final shot went in." Using the lesson's test for a real fix, which statement is true?
choices: Version 2 is not a real fix because it makes the sentences longer but does not remove a repeated opener or add a connector.
Version 2 is a real fix because it removes the repeated opener 'Everyone' and adds connectors that state relationships between the events.
Version 1 is better because short sentences make the moment feel exciting, and variety is just a matter of taste.
Version 2 is a real fix because it combines five sentences into two sentences, which always improves choppy writing.
hints: Count how many sentences in Version 1 start with 'Everyone' in a row — is that a repeated opener?
Look for the connector words in Version 2 ('when', 'and') — do they state relationships that Version 1 left for the reader to guess?

problemText: What does the removal test ask you to do when deciding whether information in a sentence is restrictive or nonrestrictive? Read the sentence and decide which step comes first.
choices: Count how many commas are in the sentence and compare that number to the number of dashes.
Cover the part in question with your thumb and read what is left to see if the sentence still points to the same person, place, or thing.
Rewrite the sentence three times, once with commas, once with parentheses, and once with dashes, then pick the version that sounds best.
Look at the part in question and count the number of words in it to determine whether it is long enough to need punctuation.
hints: The removal test is a procedure — a series of steps you follow in order.
The test involves imagining the sentence WITHOUT the part you are checking.

problemText: Jade has only one best friend, and her name is Sophia. Which sentence correctly uses commas to show that 'Sophia' is extra information, not necessary to identify who Jade means?
choices: Jade's best friend Sophia always sits with her at lunch on Thursdays.
Jade's best friend, Sophia always sits with her at lunch on Thursdays.
Jade's best friend, Sophia, always sits with her at lunch on Thursdays.
Jade's, best friend Sophia, always sits with her at lunch on Thursdays.
hints: Since Jade has only one best friend, the name is not doing identifying work — it is extra information that needs to be set off.
When extra information sits in the middle of a sentence, it needs a matching pair of marks on both sides.

problemText: The community center has three fitness classes. Which sentence correctly punctuates it so that 'the morning one' is necessary to tell which class is meant?
choices: The fitness class, the morning one, starts at six-thirty and fills up fast.
The fitness class the morning one, starts at six-thirty and fills up fast.
The fitness class the morning one starts at six-thirty and fills up fast.
The fitness class — the morning one — starts at six-thirty and fills up fast.
hints: If covering 'the morning one' would leave you unsure which of the three classes is meant, then it is restrictive and does NOT get set off.
Check each choice by covering the phrase and asking: 'Without this phrase, do I still know which class is meant?'

problemText: Zara is deciding how to punctuate two different sentences. In the first sentence, she has one hamster, and she wants to add its name, Pip, in the middle. In the second sentence, she has four cousins, and she wants to identify which one by saying 'my cousin who lives in Detroit' in the middle. How should Zara mark each sentence, and why is the marking different for the two sentences?
choices: Both sentences need a matching pair of marks around the middle information, because both pieces of information sit in the middle of the sentence and need a partner mark on each side.
The first sentence needs no commas because the name is identifying work; the second sentence needs a matching pair because the phrase is identifying work but sits in the middle.
The first sentence needs one comma because names are always set off; the second sentence needs two commas because clauses are always set off.
Neither sentence needs punctuation, because both pieces of information come after the subject and before the verb.
hints: Run the removal test on each piece of information separately: Can you remove it and still know exactly who or what is meant?
The rule about pairs is not about what kind of information it is — it is about where in the sentence the information sits.

problemText: Mr. Huang's school has one main office. He wrote: 'The main office which handles all student records stays open until five p.m.' His sentence is missing punctuation. He wants to use dashes instead of commas to set off the clause more forcefully. Which version is correct, and what rule makes his original sentence wrong?
choices: The main office — which handles all student records — stays open until five p.m., because a matching pair of marks must open and close extra information that sits in the middle.
The main office — which handles all student records stays open until five p.m., because dashes only need to go on one side when the information is nonrestrictive.
The main office, which handles all student records, stays open until five p.m., because commas work better for clauses than dashes do.
The main office which handles all student records — stays open until five p.m., because the clause is already identifying enough without a matching pair.
hints: First, run the removal test on the clause 'which handles all student records' to decide whether it is restrictive or nonrestrictive.
Then ask: when a nonrestrictive element sits in the middle of a sentence, what rule governs which punctuation marks are needed?

problemText: A student wrote five sentences about different topics and used commas or dashes in each one. Four of the five sentences are correctly punctuated according to the rules of nonrestrictive and restrictive information. One sentence has an error. Which sentence is punctuated incorrectly, and what is the specific rule it breaks?
choices: My math teacher, Ms. Chen, assigned three worksheets for homework tonight. (Ms. Chen is the only math teacher the speaker has.)
The restaurant's famous dish — grilled salmon with herbs — costs twenty dollars. (The restaurant serves many different dishes.)
Our town has one annual parade, and it always happens in July on Main Street.
The soccer team's captain, who leads practice every day, is also the team's best striker.
hints: For each sentence, ask: Is the information being set off necessary to identify what the sentence is about, or is it extra?
Then check: If the information is extra (nonrestrictive) and sits in the middle of the sentence, does it have a matching pair of marks on both sides?

problemText: What does the word 'register' mean in the context of writing? Choose the definition that matches what you learned.
choices: The adjustment of a writer's language from formal to informal depending on whether the audience is a teacher, a friend, or a stranger.
The list of people who attended an event or class and their contact information.
How formal or informal a piece of writing needs to be for its audience and purpose.
The way a writer arranges words to create rhythm and pattern in a poem or other written piece.
hints: Think about the difference between writing a school report and texting a friend.
Register determines whether you use slang and casual words or formal, careful language.

problemText:
Read the email to your school principal below. Which sentence breaks the formal register that the rest of the email uses?

'Dear Principal Chen, I am writing to request permission to start a photography club for interested sixth graders. The club would meet on Thursdays after school in the art room. Honestly, I think it would be totally awesome and super fun for everyone who likes taking pictures. The club would help students develop both artistic and technical skills.'
choices: I am writing to request permission to start a photography club for interested sixth graders.
The club would meet on Thursdays after school in the art room.
The club would help students develop both artistic and technical skills.
Honestly, I think it would be totally awesome and super fun for everyone who likes taking pictures.
hints: Look for a sentence that uses casual words or slang that do not appear in the other sentences.
Compare each sentence to the formal, careful tone of the sentences around it.

problemText:
Read the personal journal entry below. Which sentence breaks the warm, casual tone that the rest of the entry uses?

'Today was the best day ever because Maya surprised me with a birthday cake and all our friends came over to hang out. We played games for hours and laughed so hard that my face hurt. The aforementioned social gathering constituted an exceptional manifestation of amicable togetherness. I cannot believe how lucky I am to have friends like them.'
choices: The aforementioned social gathering constituted an exceptional manifestation of amicable togetherness.
Today was the best day ever because Maya surprised me with a birthday cake and all our friends came over to hang out.
We played games for hours and laughed so hard that my face hurt.
I cannot believe how lucky I am to have friends like them.
hints: Listen for stiff, formal vocabulary that sounds nothing like how a friend would naturally talk.
The casual entry uses everyday words and feelings; find the sentence that uses official-sounding terms instead.

problemText:
Read the instruction manual excerpt below, then answer the question that follows.

'To assemble the bookshelf, first lay all wooden boards on a flat surface. Next, sort the metal brackets and screws by size. Dude, you really gotta make sure all the parts are there before you start putting stuff together. Then attach the back panel using the provided nails. Finally, secure each shelf in place and allow the adhesive to dry for two hours.'

The sentence that breaks this manual's formal, instructional register could be fixed while keeping the same information. Which revision best restores consistency with the rest of the text?
choices: Dude, you should probably verify that every single component is present in the box.
Before assembling, verify that all components listed in the parts guide are present in your package.
You are gonna want to check that you have got all the pieces, trust me on this.
Make absolutely sure to inspect every single piece you got in the box before you move forward.
hints: The fix must use the same formal, careful vocabulary that appears in the other sentences of the manual.
Look for a choice that sounds like the instruction-giving tone of the sentences before and after it.

problemText:
Read the blog post excerpt below, then answer the question that follows.

'My summer at soccer camp was incredible because the coaches taught us new skills every single day. The friendships I made there were genuine and totally meaningful to me. Furthermore, the athletic training regimen implemented by the coaching staff resulted in substantial improvements to my speed and endurance. I already miss everyone and cannot wait for next summer to arrive.'

To fix the sentence that breaks this blog's warm, personal tone, you need to (1) identify which sentence does not match the casual, friendly register of the others, and (2) recognize that the problem is the register, not the grammar. Which statement correctly describes both steps?
choices: The second sentence breaks the tone because it uses words like 'genuine' and 'meaningful' that are too vague and emotional, so replace them with specific examples of the friendships instead.
The third sentence breaks the tone because it switches to stiff, formal vocabulary, even though it is a grammatically correct sentence, so rewrite it with casual, everyday words.
The first sentence breaks the tone because it uses the word 'incredible' instead of a more descriptive adjective that shows exactly what made camp special.
The fourth sentence breaks the tone because it repeats the same feeling of missing camp that appears earlier, so delete it and replace it with new information.
hints: Remember: the lesson teaches that a lapse can be a perfectly correct sentence; the problem is register, not grammar.
Look for formal vocabulary words like 'aforementioned,' 'subsequently,' or 'regimen' that stick out against everyday wording.

problemText:
Read the student research report excerpt below, then answer the question that follows.

'The Great Barrier Reef is located off the coast of Australia and covers an area of approximately 133,000 square miles. Marine biologists classify it as a system of coral ecosystems that support thousands of species. The reef is honestly so incredibly beautiful and I wish everyone could see it in person because it would totally blow their minds. Scientists estimate that rising ocean temperatures threaten approximately 50 percent of the reef's coral. Protective measures and international cooperation will be essential to preserve this natural wonder for future generations.'

To revise this report for consistency, a student must: (1) recognize which register most sentences establish, (2) identify the sentence that breaks it, (3) confirm the breaking sentence has no grammar errors, and (4) rewrite it to match the established register. Which sentence best completes this task?
choices: The reef is so incredibly beautiful because I personally find it amazing and I wish that people could visit it.
The reef is so incredibly beautiful, and many people who visit it report feeling amazed by its appearance.
The reef is honestly totally gorgeous and awesome, and it should definitely be seen by everyone in the world.
The reef is a stunning natural formation that captivates visitors with its diverse colors and intricate coral structures.
hints: The report uses careful, precise vocabulary in most sentences; the revision must match that formal, informative tone throughout.
Look for a choice that keeps the original idea (the reef's beauty and visual appeal) but expresses it with the same serious, scientific wording found in the surrounding sentences.
